# Cold induces brain region-selective cell activity-dependent lipid metabolism

## Authors

- Hyeonyoung Min<sup>1</sup>
- Yale Y Yang<sup>2</sup>

## Abstract

It has been well documented that cold is an enhancer of lipid metabolism in peripheral tissues, yet its effect on central nervous system lipid dynamics is underexplored. It is well recognized that cold acclimations enhance adipocyte functions, including white adipose tissue lipid lipolysis and beiging, and brown adipose tissue thermogenesis in mammals. However, it remains unclear whether and how lipid metabolism in the brain is also under the control of ambient temperature. Here, we show that cold exposure predominantly increases the expressions of the lipid lipolysis genes and proteins within the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH) in male mice. Mechanistically, by using innovatively combined brain-region selective pharmacology and in vivo time-lapse photometry monitoring of lipid metabolism, we find that cold activates cells within the PVH and pharmacological inactivation of cells blunts cold-induced effects on lipid peroxidation, accumulation of lipid droplets, and lipid lipolysis in the PVH. Together, these findings suggest that PVH lipid metabolism is cold sensitive and integral to cold-induced broader regulatory responses.

## Introduction

Lipid metabolism in peripheral tissues has been extensively studied, including white adipose tissue lipolysis (Grabner et al., 2021), beiging (Bartelt and Heeren, 2014), and brown adipose tissue thermogenesis Carpentier et al., 2023; however, an essential but poorly understood element is that of lipids in the central nervous system, particularly in the hypothalamus which plays a crucial role in the regulation of systematic energy metabolism (Waterson and Horvath, 2015) and glucose homeostasis (Pozo and Claret, 2018). The brain is highly thermal sensitive in that 1°C or less temperature changes can lead to functional alterations of the central nervous system (Brooks, 1983; Wang et al., 2014). Lipids provide a major source of energy and heat in the body, however, the mechanism underlying brain lipid metabolism regulations remains a mystery. There is evidence to show that the brain’s energy metabolism largely depends on the temperature (Guyton and Hall, 2006; Yu et al., 2012). We therefore assume that cold modulates brain lipid metabolism in brain regions that express the genes encoding lipid metabolic enzymes sensitive to ambient temperature. Identifying the brain regions and genes modulated by ambient temperature is of significance in our understandings of the mechanisms of maintaining brain lipid metabolism homeostasis.

Here, we combine cold exposure and brain region-selective genetic, molecular, and lipid metabolic assays, coupled with in vivo real-time two-color fiber photometry monitoring of lipid metabolic activity, to define cold-sensitive brain region(s) and lipid metabolism and to elucidate the involved cellular mechanisms.

## Results

### Cold-induced brain region-selective gene expressions of lipid lipolytic markers in males

To investigate a potential for cold exposure to modulate gene expressions for lipid lipolysis and thermogenesis in the hypothalamus, mice were exposed to a cold (4°C) chamber for 4–6 hr, a more physiologically relevant condition. Immediately after the cold challenge, mouse brains were acutely extracted and sectioned in ice-cold oxygenated artificial cerebrospinal fluids (ACSFs). Hypothalamic sections that, respectively, include the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH), lateral hypothalamus (LH), dorsomedial hypothalamus (DMH), ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), and arcuate nucleus (ARC) were transferred to ACSF-containing incubators. Micro-punches of these brain regions were subsequently made for gene assays of lipid metabolic markers.

To evaluate the effects of cold on the gene markers of lipid lipolysis, we measured the mRNA levels of two key lipolytic markers adipose triglyceride lipase (Pnpla2) and hormone-sensitive lipase (Lipe). We observed that cold-challenged male mice showed a significant increase in the gene expressions of the both of Pnpla2 (Figure 1A1) and Lipe (Figure 1A2) selectively in the PVH but not in other brain regions (Figure 1B–E). We also assayed the gene expressions of thermogenic marker uncoupling protein 2 (Ucp2) and additional thermogenic factors (Cidea, Prdm16). Cold did not significantly affect mRNA expressions of these thermogenic markers in all the examined regions in this study (Figure 1). Cold did not significantly affect gene expressions of these lipolytic and thermogenic markers in female mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). These results suggest that cold exposure (4–6 hr) could induce a rapid lipolytic activity to release fatty acids primarily in the PVH in males. Because cold did not significantly affect lipolytic markers in other regions and did not affect thermogenic markers, we next focused on studying cold-induced lipid mobilization and lipolysis in the PVH in male mice.

### Cold increases the expressions of lipid lipolytic enzymes in the PVH

To verify the cold-induced effects on lipolytic gene expressions, we next stained the protein expressions of ATGL and HSL in PVH sections using antibodies against the ATGL and HSL, respectively. Matching with the gene expression results, cold-challenged mice showed significant increases in ATGL (Figure 2) and HSL (Figure 3) expressions in both neurons and astrocytes, respectively, compared to control mice.

Moreover, we examined whether and how cold modified the phosphorylation of the HSL, a key enzyme in the regulation of lipid lipolysis. After the cold exposure of cohort groups of mice, micro-punches of PVH sections were collected and directly used for western blots of phosphorylated HSL (p-HSL), HSL, and actin. Cold significantly increased activation (S660) site phosphorylation of the HSL compared to controls (Figure 4).

### Cold-induced astrocytic accumulations of lipid droplets

It is increasingly appreciated that lipid droplets (LDs), endoplasmic reticulum-derived intracellular neutral lipid storage dynamic organelles (Olzmann and Carvalho, 2019), are predominantly accumulated in adipose tissues and liver under normal physiological conditions (Murphy, 2001; Farese and Walther, 2009). Also, there is evidence to indicate that glial cells such as astrocytes and tanycytes in the brain accumulate LDs under metabolic and hypoxic stress (Geller et al., 2019; Smolič et al., 2021). A recent elegant study shows that hyperactive neurons release fatty acids from phospholipids to formulate LDs in the brain and activation of neurons promotes lipolysis by increasing cytoplasmic lipases (Ioannou et al., 2019). These findings suggest that increased cell activity and accumulated LDs probably contribute to the cold-induced increase in the lipolytic markers we observed in this study.

To probe the mechanism of the upregulation of lipolytic markers in the PVH, we evaluated the ability for cold to accumulate LDs. After the cold challenge, mouse brains were perfused, fixed, and sectioned. Hypothalamic sections containing PVH were stained using the BODIPY 493 (BD493), an LD probe which has been well developed and widely applied to measure LD number and area in fixed tissues and live cells, respectively (Spangenburg et al., 2011; Long et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2015; Geller et al., 2019; Ioannou et al., 2019; Smolič et al., 2021). Interestingly, we observed that a short-term (30 min to 1 hr) cold exposure induced an increase in the LD area in the PVH (Figure 5A–C). We verified LDs by using the cytoplasmic LD-binding protein perilipin-2 (Figure 5D–F). To define the cell type selectivity of LD accumulation induced by cold, we co-stained LDs with the BD493, astrocytes with S100b, and neurons with neuronal marker NSE, respectively, in PVH sections. We observed that cold exposure significantly increased the BD493-positive S100b-expressing astrocytes but not NSE-expressing neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with the previous reports that LDs were primarily accumulated in glial cells (Bailey et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Marschallinger et al., 2020; Smolič et al., 2021). However, a longer (4–6 hr) cold exposure reduced the number of LDs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), which might be due to cold-induced liberations of fatty acids from the LDs to mitochondria for β-oxidation.

### Cold increases Fos expressions in PVH

We next examined whether and how cold modified cell activities within the PVH. Mice were placed in a cold chamber before mouse brains were perfused and fixed. PVH sections (40 μm in thickness) were stained using anti-Fos antibodies. Mice subjected to the cold challenge showed increased expressions of the cell activity indicator Fos in the PVH as compared to control mice (Figure 6A, B).

![Figure 6.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/98353/elife-98353-fig6-v1.jpg)

**Figure 6.:** Control or cold-challenged mouse brains were perfused and fixed and sectioned. Fos in the PVH were labeled using anti-Fos antibodies. (A) Representative images of Fos signals in PVH from one control (top) and one cold-challenged mouse (bottom). (B) Group data of Fos-positive cells in PVH in control and cold-challenged mice (n = 5 each group). Data represent mean ± SEM. Student t tests were performed. **p < 0.01. Scale bars, 100 μm for (A). 3rd V, third ventricle.

### In vivo real-time fiber photometry monitoring of cold-induced lipid peroxidation

As lipid peroxidation is essential in activity-dependent accumulation of LDs (Ioannou et al., 2019), we next evaluated the capability for cold to induce lipid peroxidation. Fiber photometry has recently been applied to detect the levels of fluorescent biosensors in vivo by us (Chen et al., 2022) and others (Sun et al., 2018; Andersen et al., 2023). To achieve this goal, we took advantage of the BODIPY581/591 C11 (BD-C11) ratiometric lipid peroxidation sensor, coupled with in vivo time-lapse two-color photometry monitoring approach. We developed and validated this approach to simultaneously monitor both red and green signals in one brain region through a single implanted photometry fiber connected to a two-color photometry system, for the BD-C11 sensor as it shifts its fluorescence emission peak from 590 (red) and 510 (green) nm when the sensor is oxidized. A custom-made Optical fiber multiple Fluid injection Cannula (OmFC) implanted over PVH was used for both BD-C11 injection and photometry monitoring of the two signals in freely behaving mice. Intra-PVH injection of the BD-C11 sensor through the OmFC was performed 4 hr prior to placing the mice in a temperature-controlled chamber. Cold potently increased the BD-C11 ratio (green to red), indicating increased lipid peroxidation (Figure 7A). To verify this result, we treated mice with a lipid soluble antioxidant α-tocopherol (α-TP) to inhibit lipid peroxidation. Compared to the vehicle-treated mice (Figure 7B), prior inhibition of lipid peroxidation with the α-TP blunted the cold-induced effects on lipid peroxidation (Figure 7C). These results demonstrate that cold induces lipid peroxidation in the PVH and that our combined fiber photometry and BD-C11 approach can be reliably applied to evaluate the dynamics of brain lipid metabolism in a spatiotemporal manner.

### Lipid peroxidation is under the control of cell activity

We next sought to examine whether cell activity is required to modulate lipid peroxidation. To examine whether cold alters cell activity, we transduced PVH cells with the Ca2+ indicator GCaMP6f- and placed the PVH transduced and photometry fiber-implanted mice in a cold chamber (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). Cold exposure increased the intensity of PVH GCaMP6f signals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C), consistent with the increased Fos expressions (Figure 6). To inhibit cell activity, we utilized the GABAA receptor agonist muscimol (MUS) (Sanders and Shekhar, 1995; Barbalho et al., 2009) and glutamate receptor antagonist Kynurenic acid (KYN) (Yoshida et al., 2012). To verify the inhibitory effect of the combined two chemicals, we performed intra-PVH injection of both MUS and KYN in PVH GCaMP6f-transduced and fiber-implanted mice. Thirty minutes post the MUS and KYN administration via intra-PVH injection was able to reduce cell activity, as indicated by the decreased intensity of GCaMP6f signals, compared to vehicle treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, E).

To test whether cell inactivation could diminish cold-induced effects on lipid peroxidation, intra-PVH injections of MUS and KYN were performed 30 min before placing the previously BD-C11-injected mice in a cold chamber and performing photometry monitoring of BD-C11 signals. Administration of the MUS and KYN prevented the cold-induced increase in the BD-C11 ratio (Figure 7D), suggesting that cell activation is required for the cold-induced lipid peroxidation.

### Cell inactivation prevents cold-induced lipolysis

To evaluate lipid lipolysis in the PVH, we performed intra-PVH injections of the EnzCheck lipase substrate through an implanted OmFC. The lipase substrate shifts its fluorescence to emission peak 515 nm (green) in the presence of lipases, and we detected the green signals using our fiber photometry system in a temporal manner. Intra-PVH injection of EnzCheck lipase substrate was performed 4 hr before placing the mice in a temperature-controlled chamber. Cold induced a potent increase in the green signals generated from the lipase substrate, indicating increased lipolysis (Figure 8A, B). We injected mice with the pan-lipase inhibitor diethylumbelliferyl phosphate (DEUP) via intra-PVT injections to inhibit lipolysis. Cold-induced lipolysis was reduced with the treatment of DEUP compared to vehicle-treated mice (Figure 8C). These results are consistent with the cold-induced increase in lipolytic markers (Figures 1—4), further indicating that cold induces lipid lipolysis in the PVH by increasing cytoplastic lipases. To examine whether cell activity is required for the cold-induced lipolysis, in cohort groups of PVH-implanted mice which were treated with the lipase substrate via intra-PVH injections, we performed intra-PVH injections of the MUS and KYN 30 min before placing the mice in a cold chamber. Administration of MUS and KYN prevented the cold-induced conversion of the lipase substrate, indicating decreased lipolytic activity (Figure 8D). These findings suggest that cold induces a rapid cell activity-dependent lipid lipolytic effect.

### Cell inactivation reduces cold-induced LD accumulation

To verify our results of LDs detected in the fixed tissues (Figure 5), we next performed time-lapse photometry monitoring of dynamics of LDs in vivo in freely behaving mice. To achieve this goal, we implanted an OmFC cannula in PVH for LD marker BD493 (green) injections and monitoring in mice. Matching with the results collected from the fixed sections, cold induced an increase in the intensity of BD493 signals (Figure 9A, B). This result indicates that cold increases the formation and accumulation of LDs, which could be directly used for lipolysis by releasing fatty acids to mitochondria for β-oxidation. The lipid soluble antioxidant α-TP blocked the cold-induced LD accumulation (Figure 9C). To define a role of cell activity in modulating LDs, we performed intra-cannula injections of both MUS and KYN in BD493-injected mice in the PVH. MUS and KYN administration blunted the cold-induced accumulation of LDs, as cold failed to increase the BD493 signals in MUS- and KYN-treated mice compared to controls (Figure 9D).

## Discussion

For survival, it is crucial for individuals to precisely modulate lipid metabolism in both the peripheral tissues and brain in mammalian animals. Extensively studies have been focused on lipid metabolism in peripheral tissues particularly in adipose tissues, while little or nothing was known about that in the brain. This was probably in part because of limited techniques. By taking advantage of combined coordinated neurobiology methods and lipid metabolic assays, we provided in this study the in vivo evidence that cold is capable to induce acute cell activity-dependent central nervous system lipid metabolic activities, including lipid peroxidation and mobilization, LD formation, and lipid lipolysis in the hypothalamus. These results fill in a missing but important gap in our understanding of brain region-selective lipid metabolism in physiological conditions, such as cold applied in this study. Also, our in vivo time-lapse fiber photometry approach detecting probe-labeled lipid metabolites would provide a powerful alternative method or technique to evaluate the dynamics of lipid metabolism in live animals. We believe that our studies will also be paradigmatic for understanding abnormal lipid metabolism in brain regions that modify energy metabolism in metabolic disorders such as obesity and diabetes.

The third ventricle adjacent PVH is a conserved brain region (Machluf et al., 2011), composed of different cell populations including those multiple brain regions-projecting parvocellular neurons and magnocellular neurons. Particularly, PVH plays varied crucial roles in modulating the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis and the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid (HPT) axis (Swanson and Sawchenko, 1983). This determines a key role of the PVH in modulating body functions, energy metabolism and glucose homeostasis in health and disease. Our findings in this study show that cold increases the expressions levels of Fos, lipid peroxidation, LD accumulation, and lipolytic markers in the PVH. These findings reveal a new role for the PVH in preventing fatty acid toxicity in pathological conditions and in integrating cold-induced broader regulatory responses.

Activated neurons would induce phospholipid peroxidation to release toxic fatty acids. One recent study (Ioannou et al., 2019) shows that nearby astrocytes have the capacity to endocytose neuron-released fatty acids, store fatty acids in LDs, and liberate fatty acids from LDs through lipolytic processes to mitochondria for β-oxidation. Consistently, our data in this study demonstrate that cold-induced lipid peroxidation and lipolysis in the brain are also under the control of cell activities. Our data show that cold increases expressions of ATGL and HSL in both neurons and astrocytes (Figures 2 and 3). These findings suggest that neurons and astrocytes communicate and interact each other to modulate lipid metabolism and prevent fatty acid accumulations in the brain in certain physiological and pathological conditions.

Lastly, the brain is highly thermal sensitive (Brooks, 1983). Identifying brain regions sensitive to ambient temperature is significant and important in our understandings of brain energy metabolism and homeostasis, as which might provide potential targetable sites in the treatment of brain lipid metabolism-associated neurological and psychological disorders.

## Materials and methods

The experimental protocol (#00001306) was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine and conducted following the U.S. National Institutes of Health guidelines for animal research.

### Animals

C57/BL6J wild-type mice (#000664, Jackson Laboratory) have been described previously and are available from The Jackson Laboratory. Both male and female mice (age 8–12 weeks) were used at the start of experiments. Mice were group-housed 3–5 mice per cage in humidity- and temperature (22–25°C)-controlled rooms on a 12-hr light:dark cycle (lights on from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.) with ad libitum access to water and mouse regular chow (#5001, LabDiet). Mice were single-caged after they received viral transductions with or without guide or optic fiber cannula insertion until all the experimental procedures were finished.

### Pharmacology

All the chemicals were purchased from Sigma except where noted. For the experiments requiring intra-PVH injections, an injector with 1 mm extension beyond the custom-made OmFC (Doric Lens) implanted over the PVH was attached by polyethylene tubing to a Hamilton syringe. The injection was performed at a speed of 50 nl per min for 4 min using a matched fluid injector consisting of a 1.25-mm ferrule and a sleeve connector, and the injector was withdrawn 10 min after the final injection. Grip cement (DENTSPLY) was used to anchor the cannula to the skull, and a plug was inserted to keep the cannula from becoming clogged when the injector was not in place. Mice were then returned to the home cage for 1 week at least before the experiments. The amount for intra-PVH injection was 200 nl of vehicle or chemicals (in μM): 100 BODIPY 493/503 (D3922, Invitrogen), 100 BODIPY 581/591 C11 (D3861, Invitrogen), 1 MitoSOX Mitochondrial Superoxide Indicators (M36005, Invitrogen), 1 EnzChek Lipase Substrate 505/515 (E33955, Invitrogen), 100 DEUP (D7692, Sigma), and 500 α-Tocopherol (#258024, Sigma); or 200 nl of 250 pmol Muscimol (M1523, Sigma) and 100 mol Kynurenic acid (K3375, Sigma).

### Stereotaxic OmFC implantations for intra-PVH injections and photometry

Following our previously documented protocols (Chen et al., 2022), mice were anesthetized with 3% isoflurane to induce the anesthesia and with 1.5–2.0% isoflurane to maintain anesthesia during the surgery and placed in a stereotaxic frame (Kopf Instruments). A small incision was made in the skin of the head, a small hole was drilled on the skull, and mice were implanted with a customer-made OmFC (Doric Lens) over the PVH (coordinates from bregma: AP –0.8 mm, 0.2 mm from midline, DV –4.0 mm). The cannula was fixed to the skull with stainless steel screws and dental cement. After the surgery, all mice received meloxicam (5 mg/kg) and continued to be housed individually. Two weeks after surgery, the mice were briefly anesthetized and inserted with the fluid injector (with 1 mm protrusion) into PVH. For intra-PVH injection, the injector was attached to a Hamilton syringe through a polyethylene tube and the mice received 200 nl of vehicle, chemicals as listed in the Pharmacology section, or viral vectors (AAV5-CamKII-GCaMP6f-WPRE-SV40, addgene#100834, titer, 2.3 × 1013 GC/ml), at a rate of 50 nl/min.

Briefly, mice were first placed in a cold chamber (4°C) for 30 min or 4–6 hr, respectively, as described in the text and figure legends. After the cold exposure, mice were deeply anesthetized with isoflurane and decapitated. ### Two-color two-channel fiber photometry

Briefly, three excitation wavelengths were used: 560, 505/490, and 405 nm. Excitation lights were generated through fiber-coupled two connectorized LEDs (CLED_560 for 560 nm; CLED_505/490 for 505 or 490 nm; CLE_405 for 405 nm; Doric Lenses) driven by a four-channel LED driver (LEDD_4; Doric Lenses). The LEDD_4 was controlled by a fiber photometry console (Doric Lenses) connected to a computer. Excitation lights were passed through two fluorescence MiniCubes (iFMC6_IE(400-410)_E1(460-490)_F1(500-540)_E2(555-570)_F2(580-680)_S)-6 ports with two integrated photodetector heads. The single detector measures both signals within the fluorescence detection windows from 500 to 540 nm and 580 to 680 nm band. The combined excitation light was sent into a patch cord made of a 400-µm core, 0.48 NA, low-autofluorescence optical fiber (Doric Lenses). The patch cord was connected to the implanted OmFC consisting of a 1.25-mm diameter optic fiber via a sleeve (Doric Lenses; Zirconia Sleeve 1.25 mm with black cover; Sleeve_ZR_1.25-BK). Both green and red fluorescence signals were collected through the same patch cord and passed through the same Minicube and focused onto a Fluorescence Detector Head (FDH; Doric Lenses). The photometry experiments were run in a Lock-in mode, and the acquisition rate was set to 12.0 ksps*C controlled by Doric Neuroscience Studio software (Doric Lenses). The fiber photometry experiments were performed 5 min after connecting the optic fibers to the animals. We processed the signals using the Doric Neuroscience Studio software (V5.3.3.14) to calculate the normalized fluorescence variation of the images (ΔF/F), and averaged the signals at 1 s bins. To avoid or minimize bleaching over time, we performed patch cord photobleaching for 12 hr before each experiment, reduced the illumination power outputs as much as possible, and recorded the signals for 30 s every 5 min. We used a rotary joint for long-term photometry recordings in freely moving animals.

### Brain histology and immunofluorescence

Mice were euthanized and transcardially perfused with 1× phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4) followed by 4% paraformaldehyde in phosphate buffer (PFA, pH 7.2). Mouse brains were removed and post-fixed in 4% PFA overnight. Fixed brains were transferred to 30% sucrose in PFA for cryoprotection for three days. Next, 30 μm coronal sections were cut in a freezing cryostat (Leica).

For immunofluorescence, slices were washed three times in 1× PBS for 10 min each and heat incubated with target antigen retrieval solution (Invitrogen) for 2 min at 95°C. And then, the slices were washed three times in 1× PBS for 10 min each, followed by permeabilization in 1% Triton X-100 solution in 1× PBS for 40 min at room temperature. After blocking for 1 hr at room temperature, the slices were incubated with a mouse Fos antibody (1:150, sc-166940 AF647, Santa Cruz Biotechnologies), rabbit ATGL (1:150, bs-3831R-BF488, Bioss), rabbit HSL (1:150, bs-3223R-BF488, Bioss), rabbit NSE (1:200, bs-10445R-BF594, Bioss), and mouse S100b (1:200, bsm-10832-BF594, Bioss), respectively, for overnight at 4°C in the dark. The slices were then rinsed three times in 0.1% Triton X-100 solution in 1× PBS for 10 min each. For LD staining, slices were washed three times in 1× PBS for 10 min each and then incubated with 1% Triton X-100 solution in 1× PBS for 40 min. After blocking for 1 hr, the slices were stained with 20 μg/ml BODIPY 493/503 (Invitrogen, D3922) for 4 hr at room temperature in the dark. After the incubation, the slices were rinsed three times in 0.1% Triton X-100 solution in 1× PBS for 10 min each.

For BODIPY 493/503 co-staining with perilipin-2, NSE, and S100b, respectively, after permeabilization in 1% Triton X-100 solution in 1× PBS for 40 min and blocking for 1 hr at room temperature, the slices were incubated with rabbit perilipin-2 (1:200, CL594-15294, Proteintech), rabbit NSE, and mouse S100b antibodies, respectively, for overnight at 4°C in the dark. The slices were then washed three times in 0.1% Triton X-100 solution in 1× PBS for 10 min and incubated with 20 μg/ml BODIPY 493/503 (Invitrogen, D3922) for 4 hr at room temperature in the dark and then washed three times in 0.1% Triton X-100 solution in 1× PBS for 10 min each time. The stained slices were dried and mounted with mounting medium (0100-20, Southern Biotech). Images were taken using the All-in-One Fluorescence Microscope (BZ-X800E Keyence) and analyzed using the BZ-X800 Analyzer (Keyence).

### PVH tissue western blot

Acute coronal brain slices (260 μm thickness) were collected following the procedures as stated in the above. Six micro-punches of PVH sections from each mouse were made and immediately placed in 40 μl cold lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris–HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 0.25% Na-deoxycholate, 1 mM EDTA, 1% NP-40, 1 mM PMSF (20 mM PMSF in 100% ethanol), and 1 protease inhibitor tablet (A32955, Thermo Scientific). The samples were homogenized in lysis buffer and centrifuged at 14,000 × rpm at 4°C for 20 min. The supernatants were transferred to a fresh tube and used for Bradford assay to quantify the protein concentration. Equal amounts of protein from each sample were denatured and boiled at 100°C for 5 min. Proteins were separated by electrophoresis in 10% SDS–PAGE gel and transferred to PVDF membrane. The membrane was blocked with Protein-Free blocking buffer (927-80001, LI-COR) for 1 hr and incubated overnight with relevant primary antibodies at 4°C, including the p-HSL (1:1000, PA5-64494, Invitrogen), HSL (1:1000, PA5-17196, Invitrogen), and β-actin (1:5000, MAB8929, R&D Systems). After washing in PBS-Tween 20 (PBST), the membranes were incubated with secondary antibodies for 1 hr and a subsequent PBST washing. Images were acquired using Odyssey Classic Imager (LI-COR). The band intensity of HSL and p-HSL was quantified using the ImageJ.

### Statistics and reproducibility

Animals were randomly assigned to experimental or control groups. Following post hoc histological conformation of viral transfections and cannula/fiber placements, all mice with inaccurate viral infections or cannula placements were excluded from behavior experiments. All experiments were repeated at least twice, and data represent the technical and biological replicates. Paired or unpaired Student’s t tests were used to analyze differences between two groups of the same or different mice when appropriate, respectively. One-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test was used to compare group data from more than two groups of mice. Two-way ANOVA was used to analyze data from more than two groups across various time points. All data were analyzed by using Prism 10.0 (GraphPad Software).

This phenomenological study reported that cold exposure induced mRNA expression of genes related to lipid metabolism in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH). While the paper does not address cell-type specificity or the functional role of lipids in PVH, the findings might still serve as a useful basis for others to explore their relevance to brain responses to cold. In the revised manuscript, the authors made adequate editions, such as new immunostaining and immunoblotting of AGTL and HSL in the PVH, and pharmacological inhibition of lipid peroxidation and lipolysis. ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.98353.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.98353.3.sa1)

Summary:

This study focuses on metabolic changes in the paraventricular hypothalamic (PVH) region of the brain during acute periods of cold exposure. The authors point out that in comparison to the extensive literature on the effects of cold exposure in peripheral tissues, we know relatively little about its effects on the brain. They specifically focus on the hypothalamus, and identify the PVH as having changes in Atgl and Hsl gene expression changes during cold exposure. They then go on to show accumulation of lipid droplets, increased Fos expression, and increased lipid peroxidation during cold exposure. Further, they show that neuronal activation is required for the formation of lipid droplets and lipid peroxidation.

Strengths:

A strength of the study is trying to better understand how metabolism in the brain is a dynamic process, much like how it has been viewed in other organs. The authors also use a creative approach to measuring in vivo lipid peroxidation via delivery of BD-C11 sensor through a cannula to the region in conjunction with fiber photometry to measure fluorescence changes deep in the brain.

Comments on revised version:

The authors have attempted to address concerns brought to their attention in the initial review. They have performed one or two additional experiments to address concerns (e.g. adding fiber photometry of PVH neurons and trying to manipulate lipid peroxidation) though many of the concerns from the original review stand. The authors have also revised the text to limit the extent of their claims and to improve clarity, which is appreciated.

results.result: Cold exposure (4-6 hr) selectively increases lipolytic gene expression (Pnpla2 and Lipe) in the PVH of male mice but not in other hypothalamic regions (LH, DMH, VMH, ARC) or in female mice. Thermogenic markers (Ucp2, Cidea, Prdm16) were not affected by cold in any examined region.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C22 are well-supported by qPCR data in Figure 1 showing statistically significant increases in Pnpla2 and Lipe specifically in male PVH (p<0.05 and p<0.01), with no significant changes in other regions or in females. The regional and sex specificity is clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistical testing and adequate sample sizes (n=6-12 per group).

results.result: Cold exposure increases protein expression of lipolytic enzymes ATGL and HSL in both neurons and astrocytes in the PVH, and increases activating phosphorylation of HSL at Ser660.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figures 2-3) showing significant increases in ATGL and HSL colocalization with both neuronal (NSE) and astrocytic (S100b) markers (p<0.001, p<0.05), and western blot data (Figure 4) demonstrating increased p-HSL(Ser660) (p<0.01, n=6). These findings confirm the gene expression results at the protein level.

results.result: Short-term cold exposure (30 min-1 hr) increases lipid droplet accumulation specifically in astrocytes in the PVH, while longer exposure (4-6 hr) reduces LD numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are supported by BODIPY 493 staining data showing significant LD area increase after short cold exposure (Figure 5A-C, p<0.0001, n=6) with astrocyte-specific accumulation (Figure 5—supplement 1, p<0.05), and reduction after longer exposure (Figure 5—supplement 2, p<0.0419). The biphasic temporal pattern is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Cold exposure activates PVH cells as demonstrated by increased Fos expression and elevated GCaMP6f calcium signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C7, and C38 are supported by immunofluorescence showing increased Fos-positive cells (Figure 6, p<0.01, n=5) and fiber photometry showing elevated GCaMP6f signals during cold exposure (Figure 7—supplement 1B-C, n=4). These converging lines of evidence demonstrate cold-induced cellular activation in the PVH.

results.result: Cold induces lipid peroxidation in the PVH in a cell activity-dependent manner, as demonstrated by increased BD-C11 ratio that is blocked by antioxidant α-TP or pharmacological cell inactivation with MUS+KYN.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 are supported by fiber photometry data showing cold-induced increases in BD-C11 ratio (Figure 7A-B, n=6) that are prevented by α-TP (Figure 7C, n=4) or MUS+KYN treatment (Figure 7D, n=4). The pharmacological rescue experiments with validated cell inactivation (Figure 7—supplement 1D-E) provide strong evidence for cell activity dependence.

results.result: Cold induces rapid cell activity-dependent lipolysis in the PVH, as shown by increased lipase substrate conversion that is reduced by lipase inhibitor DEUP or cell inactivation with MUS+KYN.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 are supported by fiber photometry data showing cold-induced increases in EnzCheck lipase substrate fluorescence (Figure 8A-B, n=4) that are blocked by DEUP (Figure 8C, n=4) or MUS+KYN (Figure 8D, n=4). The pharmacological controls validate that the signal reflects lipase activity and requires cell activation.

results.result: Cold-induced lipid droplet accumulation in the PVH is blocked by antioxidant α-TP or cell inactivation with MUS+KYN, as measured by in vivo fiber photometry of BODIPY 493 signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are supported by fiber photometry data showing cold-induced increases in BD493 signals (Figure 9A-B, n=4) that are prevented by α-TP (Figure 9C, n=4) or MUS+KYN (Figure 9D, n=6). This validates the fixed tissue findings and demonstrates that LD accumulation depends on lipid peroxidation and cell activity.

results.result: Intra-PVH injection of MUS and KYN reduces cell activity 30 minutes post-administration as measured by decreased GCaMP6f signals.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 is supported by GCaMP6f photometry data (Figure 7—supplement 1D-E) showing significant reduction in calcium spike frequency after MUS+KYN treatment compared to vehicle (p<0.05, n=3 per group). This validates the pharmacological approach used in subsequent experiments.

results.result: The combined fiber photometry and BD-C11 approach can reliably evaluate dynamics of brain lipid metabolism in a spatiotemporal manner.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by the validation experiments showing that the BD-C11 ratiometric sensor responds to cold-induced lipid peroxidation (Figure 7A) and is blocked by the antioxidant α-TP (Figure 7C), demonstrating specificity. The technical approach is well-described and produces interpretable, reproducible results across multiple experiments.

results.result: PVH lipid metabolism is cold sensitive and integral to cold-induced broader regulatory responses, as evidenced by coordinated increases in Fos expression, lipid peroxidation, LD accumulation, and lipolytic markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 and C53 represent integrative conclusions supported by the collective experimental findings (Figures 1-9). The cold sensitivity is clearly demonstrated, though the claim about integration with "broader regulatory responses" (C12) is somewhat speculative as direct connections to systemic physiology were not tested. The core conclusion about cold-sensitive PVH lipid metabolism is well-supported.

results.result: The reduction in LDs after longer cold exposure and the functional role of accumulated LDs in providing fatty acids for β-oxidation are proposed mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C34 and C71 are explicitly speculative ("might be due to", "could be directly used for") and lack direct experimental evidence. While the biphasic LD dynamics are observed (C33 supported), the mechanistic interpretation regarding β-oxidation is not tested. Measurements of fatty acid flux, mitochondrial β-oxidation, or metabolic tracing would be needed to support these mechanistic claims.

results.result: The PVH has roles in preventing fatty acid toxicity in pathological conditions, integrating cold-induced regulatory responses, and facilitating neuron-astrocyte communication to modulate lipid metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 and C59 are speculative interpretations extending beyond the experimental data. While the study demonstrates cold-induced lipid metabolic changes in the PVH, no pathological conditions were tested (C54), systemic integration was not directly measured (C55), and neuron-astrocyte communication was inferred rather than demonstrated (C59). These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not supported by the current data.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about cold effects on peripheral lipid metabolism, hypothalamic function, brain thermal sensitivity, lipid droplet biology, and neuron-astrocyte lipid metabolism are stated as established facts supported by citations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C13-C17, C26-C29, C32, C50-C52, C56, C60, C63-C64, and C67 represent background knowledge appropriately supported by citations to prior literature. These claims provide context for the current work and are not primary findings of this study. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: Identifying temperature-sensitive brain regions is significant for understanding brain energy metabolism and may provide therapeutic targets for lipid metabolism-associated neurological disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are speculative statements about the broader significance and potential therapeutic applications of the research. While the identification of the PVH as temperature-sensitive is supported by the data, the translational implications for treating neurological disorders are entirely speculative and not tested in this study.

results.result: Cold exposure predominantly increases expressions of lipid lipolysis genes and proteins in the PVH of male mice, inducing rapid lipolytic activity to release fatty acids.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C66 summarize the main findings supported by Figures 1-4. The gene expression (qPCR), protein expression (immunofluorescence), and protein activation (western blot) data collectively demonstrate cold-induced upregulation of lipolytic machinery specifically in the male PVH. The interpretation of "rapid lipolytic activity" is supported by the 4-6 hr timeframe and functional assays.

results.result: Pharmacological cell inactivation blunts cold-induced lipid peroxidation, LD accumulation, and lipolysis in the PVH, demonstrating that these processes are under cell activity control.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 and C57 are supported by the MUS+KYN pharmacological rescue experiments shown in Figures 7D, 8D, and 9D. The consistent blocking effect across multiple lipid metabolic readouts provides strong evidence for cell activity dependence. However, the pharmacological approach lacks cell-type specificity, so whether neurons, astrocytes, or both are required remains unclear.

results.result: Cold induces lipid lipolysis in the PVH by increasing cytoplasmic lipases (ATGL and HSL) in both neurons and astrocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C44 and C58 integrate findings from gene expression (C18-C19), protein expression (C23-C24), phosphorylation (C25), and functional lipase activity (C42-C43) data. The conclusion that cold increases cytoplasmic lipases is well-supported. The presence of these enzymes in both cell types is demonstrated by colocalization studies, though the relative contributions of each cell type to overall lipolysis are not quantified.

results.result: Methodological claims about experimental design rationale and biosensor properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C65, C68, and C70 describe methodological choices and biosensor properties. C65 states that 4-6 hr cold exposure is "more physiologically relevant" but provides no justification for this assertion. C68 and C70 accurately describe the spectral properties of the BD-C11 and EnzCheck sensors, which are established commercial reagents. These are minor methodological details rather than primary findings.

results.result: Cold exposure selectively increases gene expression of lipolytic markers (Pnpla2 and Lipe) in the PVH of male mice but not in other hypothalamic regions or in female mice. Thermogenic markers (Ucp2, Cidea, Prdm16) were not affected by cold in any examined region.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'these studies are solid in conclusively describing how the PVH is reprogrammed at the level of gene expression by cold exposure.' The editor's summary confirms that 'cold exposure induced mRNA expression of genes related to lipid metabolism in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH)' and that the findings are 'solid.'

results.result: Cold exposure increases protein expression of ATGL and HSL in both neurons and astrocytes in the PVH, as demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining.
results.evaluation: The editor's summary notes that 'the authors made adequate editions, such as new immunostaining...of AGTL and HSL in the PVH' in response to reviewer concerns. The anonymous reviewer acknowledges these additions were performed to address initial concerns, indicating acceptance of this data.

results.result: Cold exposure increases the activating phosphorylation (S660) of HSL in the PVH, indicating enhanced lipolytic enzyme activity.
results.evaluation: The editor's summary mentions 'new...immunoblotting of AGTL and HSL in the PVH' as adequate additions made by the authors. This phosphorylation data is part of the immunoblotting experiments that reviewers found acceptable, with no specific critique raised.

results.result: Short-term cold exposure (30 min to 1 hr) increases lipid droplet accumulation in the PVH, primarily in astrocytes rather than neurons, while longer exposure (4-6 hr) reduces lipid droplet numbers.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that the authors 'show accumulation of lipid droplets...during cold exposure' as a strength. The temporal dynamics and cell-type specificity are presented as descriptive findings that reviewers accept, though they note 'the paper does not address cell-type specificity' as a limitation of functional interpretation rather than data validity.

results.result: Cold exposure activates PVH cells, as demonstrated by increased Fos expression and GCaMP6f calcium signals.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly states the authors 'show...increased Fos expression...during cold exposure' and notes they added 'fiber photometry of PVH neurons' to address concerns. The editor confirms these additions were adequate, indicating acceptance of the neuronal activation data.

results.result: Cold induces lipid peroxidation in the PVH, which can be blocked by the antioxidant α-TP or by pharmacological inactivation of cells with MUS and KYN, demonstrating that cell activation is required for cold-induced lipid peroxidation.
results.evaluation: The editor notes 'pharmacological inhibition of lipid peroxidation' as an adequate addition. The anonymous reviewer acknowledges the authors 'performed one or two additional experiments to address concerns (e.g....trying to manipulate lipid peroxidation)' and that these experiments were attempted, indicating acceptance of the approach and findings.

results.result: Cold induces lipolysis in the PVH as measured by lipase substrate conversion, which is reduced by the lipase inhibitor DEUP and prevented by pharmacological cell inactivation with MUS and KYN, indicating cell activity-dependent lipolysis.
results.evaluation: The editor's summary states 'pharmacological inhibition of...lipolysis' was an adequate addition. The anonymous reviewer notes the authors use 'a creative approach to measuring in vivo lipid peroxidation via delivery of BD-C11 sensor through a cannula to the region in conjunction with fiber photometry' as a strength, which applies to the lipolysis measurements as well.

results.result: Cold-induced lipid droplet accumulation in the PVH can be blocked by the antioxidant α-TP or by pharmacological cell inactivation with MUS and KYN, demonstrating that both lipid peroxidation and cell activity are required for LD formation.
results.evaluation: These findings are part of the pharmacological manipulation experiments that the editor deemed 'adequate' and that the anonymous reviewer acknowledged were performed to address concerns. The mechanistic connection between cell activity, lipid peroxidation, and LD accumulation is accepted as part of the overall phenomenological description.

results.result: Intra-PVH injection of MUS and KYN reduces PVH cell activity as measured by decreased GCaMP6f signals.
results.evaluation: This validation of the pharmacological approach is implicitly accepted as part of the reviewers' acknowledgment that the authors 'performed one or two additional experiments' including manipulation attempts. The editor's acceptance of the pharmacological inhibition experiments indicates this control was deemed adequate.

results.result: PVH lipid metabolism is cold-sensitive, with cold-induced lipid peroxidation and lipolysis being under the control of cell activities, representing a rapid lipolytic response primarily in the PVH of males.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states 'the reviewers considered that these studies are solid in conclusively describing how the PVH is reprogrammed at the level of gene expression by cold exposure.' The anonymous reviewer acknowledges this as a 'phenomenological study' that provides solid descriptive findings about PVH responses to cold.

results.result: PVH lipid metabolism is integral to cold-induced broader regulatory responses, with the PVH playing a role in preventing fatty acid toxicity and integrating cold responses through neuron-astrocyte communication.
results.evaluation: The editor notes 'the paper does not address...the functional role of lipids in PVH' as a limitation, though 'the findings might still serve as a useful basis for others to explore their relevance to brain responses to cold.' The anonymous reviewer states 'many of the concerns from the original review stand' and notes the authors 'revised the text to limit the extent of their claims,' suggesting these broader functional interpretations remain speculative.

results.result: The combined fiber photometry and BD-C11 approach can reliably evaluate the dynamics of brain lipid metabolism in a spatiotemporal manner.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly praises this as a strength: 'The authors also use a creative approach to measuring in vivo lipid peroxidation via delivery of BD-C11 sensor through a cannula to the region in conjunction with fiber photometry to measure fluorescence changes deep in the brain.'

results.result: Background claims about cold effects on peripheral tissues, hypothalamic function, brain thermal sensitivity, lipid droplet biology, and technical properties of fluorescent probes.
results.evaluation: These are established background facts cited from the literature that reviewers do not question. They provide context for the study but are not novel findings being evaluated.

results.result: Speculative interpretations about the functional significance of findings, including potential therapeutic applications and the physiological relevance of experimental conditions.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer notes 'the authors have also revised the text to limit the extent of their claims,' suggesting these speculative statements were toned down but remain somewhat uncertain. The editor's comment that the paper 'does not address...the functional role of lipids in PVH' indicates these functional interpretations are not fully supported.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations find strong support for claims C18-C22 regarding cold-induced gene expression changes in the PVH. OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation (p-values, sample sizes), while peer reviewers describe the findings as 'solid' and 'conclusively describing how the PVH is reprogrammed at the level of gene expression.' Both also address C5-C6 (OpenEval R15, Peer R1), with complete agreement on the quality of gene expression data.

Both evaluations support claims C23-C24 regarding ATGL and HSL protein expression. OpenEval provides detailed statistical analysis of immunofluorescence and western blot data, while peer reviewers note these were 'adequate additions' made in response to initial concerns. Peer R2 also addresses C58 (covered in OpenEval R17), indicating acceptance of the protein-level validation.

Both evaluations support claim C25 regarding HSL phosphorylation. OpenEval cites specific western blot data (p<0.01, n=6), while peer reviewers mention 'immunoblotting of AGTL and HSL' as adequate additions with no specific critique raised.

Perfect agreement on claims C30-C33 regarding lipid droplet accumulation dynamics. OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation of BODIPY staining data showing biphasic temporal patterns, while peer reviewers note the authors 'show accumulation of lipid droplets...during cold exposure' as a strength and accept the descriptive findings.

Perfect agreement on claims C7, C35, C38 regarding cold-induced cellular activation. OpenEval cites Fos immunofluorescence and GCaMP6f photometry data with statistics, while peer reviewers explicitly state the authors 'show...increased Fos expression...during cold exposure' and added 'fiber photometry of PVH neurons' as adequate additions.

Strong agreement on claims C36-C37, C40-C41 regarding lipid peroxidation and its dependence on cell activity. OpenEval details BD-C11 photometry data with pharmacological controls, while peer reviewers note 'pharmacological inhibition of lipid peroxidation' as adequate and acknowledge the manipulation experiments were performed to address concerns. Peer R6 also addresses C8 (covered in OpenEval R16).

Strong agreement on claims C42-C43, C45-C46 regarding lipase activity measurements. OpenEval provides detailed EnzCheck photometry data with pharmacological controls, while peer reviewers state 'pharmacological inhibition of...lipolysis' was adequate and praise the 'creative approach to measuring in vivo' using fiber photometry. Peer R7 also addresses C10, C44 (covered in OpenEval R16, R17).

Strong agreement on claims C47-C49 regarding lipid droplet accumulation dependence on lipid peroxidation and cell activity. OpenEval details BD493 photometry with pharmacological controls, while peer reviewers accept these as part of the 'adequate' pharmacological manipulation experiments. Peer R8 also addresses C9 (covered in OpenEval R16).

Perfect agreement on claim C39 regarding validation of the MUS+KYN pharmacological approach. OpenEval cites specific GCaMP6f data showing reduced calcium spike frequency (p<0.05), while peer reviewers implicitly accept this validation as part of their acknowledgment that manipulation experiments were performed and deemed adequate.

Perfect agreement on claim C69 regarding the BD-C11 biosensor validation. OpenEval describes the technical validation and specificity controls, while peer reviewers explicitly praise this as a strength: 'a creative approach to measuring in vivo lipid peroxidation via delivery of BD-C11 sensor through a cannula.'

Both evaluations support claims C11, C53 regarding the core conclusion about cold-sensitive PVH lipid metabolism. OpenEval notes the findings are well-supported but C12 is 'somewhat speculative,' while peer reviewers state the studies are 'solid in conclusively describing how the PVH is reprogrammed' but note limitations in addressing functional roles. Peer R10 also addresses C57, C66 (covered in OpenEval R16, R15).

Both evaluations rate claims C34, C71 as uncertain/speculative. OpenEval states these mechanistic interpretations regarding β-oxidation 'lack direct experimental evidence,' while peer reviewers note 'the authors have also revised the text to limit the extent of their claims' and that the paper 'does not address...the functional role of lipids.' Peer R14 also addresses C61-C62, C65 (covered in OpenEval R14, R18).

Both evaluations rate claims C54-C55, C59 as uncertain/speculative. OpenEval states these are 'speculative interpretations extending beyond the experimental data' representing 'reasonable hypotheses for future work,' while peer reviewers note 'many of the concerns from the original review stand' and the paper 'does not address...the functional role of lipids in PVH,' though findings 'might still serve as a useful basis for others.'

Perfect agreement on claims C1-C4, C13-C17, C26-C29, C32, C50-C52, C56, C60, C63-C64, C67 as established background knowledge appropriately cited from literature. OpenEval notes these 'provide context for the current work and are not primary findings,' while peer reviewers do not question these established facts. Peer R13 also includes C68, C70 (covered in OpenEval R18).

Both evaluations rate claims C61-C62 as uncertain regarding therapeutic applications. OpenEval states these are 'entirely speculative and not tested in this study,' while peer reviewers note the authors 'revised the text to limit the extent of their claims' and that functional interpretations are not fully supported. This overlaps with peer assessment of C34, C65, C71 (covered in OpenEval R11, R18).

Both evaluations support claims C5-C6 summarizing main findings on cold-induced lipolytic machinery upregulation. OpenEval integrates data from Figures 1-4 and notes the interpretation of 'rapid lipolytic activity' is supported, while peer reviewers describe the gene expression findings as 'solid.' This complements the agreement on C18-C22 in the primary pairing (OpenEval R1, Peer R1).

Both evaluations support claims C8-C10 regarding cell activity dependence of lipid metabolism. OpenEval cites MUS+KYN pharmacological rescue experiments across multiple readouts but notes lack of cell-type specificity, while peer reviewers accept the pharmacological inhibition experiments as adequate. Peer R6 focuses on C36-C37, C40-C41, C8 while OpenEval R16 addresses C8-C10, C57.

Partial overlap on claim C10 regarding cell activity dependence. OpenEval R16 supports this through MUS+KYN experiments, while peer R7 accepts the pharmacological inhibition of lipolysis as adequate. Peer R7 primarily focuses on C42-C46, C10, C44 while OpenEval R16 addresses C8-C10, C57.

Partial overlap on claim C9 regarding cell activity dependence of lipid droplet accumulation. OpenEval R16 supports this through pharmacological rescue data, while peer R8 accepts these findings as part of the overall phenomenological description. Peer R8 primarily focuses on C47-C49, C9 while OpenEval R16 addresses C8-C10, C57.

Partial overlap on claim C57 regarding cell activity dependence as an integrative conclusion. OpenEval R16 supports this through consistent pharmacological blocking effects, while peer R10 accepts this as part of the solid phenomenological description of PVH responses to cold.

Partial overlap on claim C58 regarding cytoplasmic lipases. OpenEval R17 integrates gene expression, protein expression, phosphorylation, and functional data to support this conclusion, while peer R2 accepts the immunostaining and immunoblotting of ATGL and HSL as adequate additions.

Partial overlap on claim C44 regarding increased cytoplasmic lipases. OpenEval R17 integrates multiple lines of evidence (C18-C19, C23-C25, C42-C43) to support this conclusion, while peer R7 accepts the lipolysis measurements and pharmacological inhibition experiments as adequate.

Partial overlap on claim C66 regarding rapid lipolytic activity. OpenEval R15 supports this interpretation based on the 4-6 hr timeframe and functional assays, while peer R10 accepts this as part of the solid phenomenological description of PVH reprogramming by cold exposure.

Partial overlap on claims C68, C70 regarding biosensor spectral properties. OpenEval R18 notes these accurately describe established commercial reagents as minor methodological details, while peer R13 accepts these as background facts that are not questioned.

Partial overlap on claim C65 regarding the 4-6 hr cold exposure timepoint. OpenEval R18 notes this claim lacks justification for being 'more physiologically relevant,' while peer R14 groups this with other speculative statements that were toned down in revision but remain somewhat uncertain.
